messages.author: d1a447e1c9bca559
messages.subject: transform multivariate data
parts:
Shalom,
I have multivariate data - matrix X with n rows and p columns
I want to do a linear transformation V=XA similar to PCA 
but maximizing the Kurtosis instead of the variance.
 
How can I do it?
 
Thank you
Ronen

messages.author: b27d618f22c908c3
messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] transform multivariate data
parts:
Hi Ronen,

Sounds like a very interesting problem. I'll be happy to hear the context if you're willing to share.

It seems like there's some literature on this problem. I found this paper which seems to describe an algorithm for solving the problem. There are references for other works with similar goals in the paper. I imagine you'll find some recipe there. I didn't find a software package, maybe Tal will google it for us :)

Personally - if your data is not too large, and if you're not going to apply the procedure too many times, I would start by writing a solver myself and seeing if it produces satisfactory results. 
Start with a random direction s s.t. |s|=1, compute the kurtosis. Then choose one coordinate and use optimize to maximize it. Iterate over the coordinates several times until convergence. If your problem is well-behaved enough (convex, I think), this should work. Otherwise other methods should have a hard time as well I think. You can try several random starting points to see if they converge to the same point. You can also try simulated annealing and such hueristics. 

I think you'd need to renormalize s after every update to keep |s|=1. Note that when you update s you don't need to compute the whole thing from scratch (X%*% s) which is heavy - if you updated coordinate i, you can just add X_i * (s_i_new- s_i_old) where X_i is the i'th row of X, and then divide the result by |s_new|. This should keep you within a reasonable running time (again, depending on the size of your data) - this will keep your complexity quadratic rather than cubic. 

David.

messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] transform multivariate data
parts:
Thank you David!
I am trying to find an algorithm for finding suspected multivariate outliers in our data sets.
I have seen the paper you referred to.
Their algorithm in section 3.1 - resulted with very correlated transformed data.
I am not sure what kind of orthogonality their algorithm is keeping.
 
There is also ICA - independent componenet analysis which has a package in R.
but this transformation maximizes the non-normality (neg-entropy) which if i understand well,
is a combination of skewness and kurtosis and therefore is not ideal for me.
 
There is the package ICS - but i didnt understand exactly what it does...
 
In the algorithm you give, how do you keep orthogonality of the projected vectors?
 
Thank you very much
Ronen

messages.author: b27d618f22c908c3
messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] transform multivariate data
parts:
Sorry - I was under the impression you're looking for a single projection, in which case there's no issue. 

I think you can solve this problem: after you have your first direction s1, you can remove the projection onto it from the data in the spirit of Gram-Schmidt: let x denote a 1Xp vector of a single observation
than x_new <- x - (<x,s1>/<s1,s1>) * s1
where <a,b> is the inner product (i.e. a %*% b in R)
This actually subtracts the projection onto s1 from each observation. Then, I think the maximizer of the next iteration is guaranteed to be orthogonal to s1.   

This is not an ideal solution and such tricks usually introduce a lot of instability to the process due to noise accumulation. so keep in mind that if you're looking for many components it will work poorly. 

a better approach numerically might be to search in the second step only for directions which are orthogonal to s1 (e.g. by running a Gram-Schmidt step using s1 and any new candidate for s2), but I think you'll have to give up the acceleration trick, (at least I can't see how not to right now).

David.
